keyTerms.definition: A model that learns a probability law over data and can sample new data.
Scores one parameter setting against fixed data.
The law that puts mass 1/n on each observed sample.
Whether distinct parameters give distinct observable laws.

recall.question: What objects does this lesson cover?
recall.answer: The objects every generative model manipulates: probability versus density, support, normalization, joint and marginal laws, sampling, likelihood, the empirical distribution, estimation, entropy, divergence, identifiability.

recall.question: What should the learner be able to do after this lesson?
recall.answer: Separate probability from density, state a support, normalize a law, move between joint and marginal forms, draw samples, score parameters with likelihood, build the empirical distribution, compute entropy and KL by hand, and spot a non-identifiable parameter.

keyTerms.definition: The twelve fixed draws (R x6, G x4, B x2) used for every number in the lesson.
The normalized counts of the toy: p_hat = (0.500, 0.333, 0.167).

recall.question: What are the fixed counts in the running toy?
recall.answer: R appears 6 times, G 4 times, B 2 times, n = 12.

recall.question: What is the empirical law of the toy?

keyTerms.definition: A number in [0,1] on a discrete outcome. All point masses sum to 1.
A non-negative curve over a continuum. Only its integrals are probabilities.
A probability assignment over countable outcomes that sums to 1.
Dividing raw counts or scores so the total mass equals 1.

recall.question: Why is 0.399 not a probability for N(0,1)?
recall.answer: 0.399 is a density value at x = 0. Only integrals of density are probabilities; the area between -0.1 and 0.1, about 0.080, is one.

recall.question: What are the normalization rules for discrete and continuous laws?
recall.answer: Discrete: point masses in [0,1] sum to 1. Continuous: density >= 0 integrates to 1.

recall.question: What goes wrong if a density integrates to 1.4?
recall.answer: Every downstream integral is wrong by the same factor, and likelihood comparisons between models become meaningless.

keyTerms.definition: The set where the density or mass is positive; outside it probability is exactly 0.
Supports with no overlap; one sample can tell the two laws apart.

recall.question: What is the support of the toy law?
recall.answer: supp(p_hat) = {R, G, B}.

recall.question: Why can two laws with disjoint supports be told apart by one sample?
recall.answer: A sample must come from its law's support. A draw possible under one law is impossible under the other.

keyTerms.definition: Z: the sum or integral of unnormalized scores that normalizes a law.
A model that keeps unnormalized scores and pays for Z at sampling time.

recall.question: What is the normalized law for scores (6,4,2)?
Why is there no free option for the partition function?
recall.answer: Energy models pay for Z at sampling time; normalized models pay at training time.

keyTerms.definition: Probability mass function: assigns probabilities to discrete outcomes.
Probability density function: assigns density to continuous outcomes.
The loss used for discrete outcomes; pairs with PMF modeling.

recall.question: When does the math sum and when does it integrate?
recall.answer: Discrete laws use PMFs and sums; continuous laws use PDFs and integrals.

recall.question: How does the variable-type choice change the likelihood?
recall.answer: It changes the likelihood formula, not the data. Cross-entropy fits discrete tokens; log-density fits continuous values.

keyTerms.definition: The full probability law over two or more variables together.
The law of one variable alone, found by summing the joint over the other.
The law of one variable inside a slice of another, renormalized.
p(a,b) = p(a) p(b|a): the joint factors into marginal times conditional.

recall.question: Compute p(S|G) and p(G|S) for the toy. Why do they differ?
recall.answer: p(S|G) = 1/4 = 0.25. p(G|S) = 1/6 = 0.1667. They condition on different slices, so mixing them up is the classic error.

recall.question: State the chain rule.
recall.answer: p(a,b) = p(a) p(b|a). Marginals sum the joint; conditionals zoom into one slice and renormalize.

keyTerms.definition: A deterministic map from a noise source to outcomes whose frequencies match the law.
A 1-D sampling method that inverts the CDF to map uniform noise to outcomes.
The wobble of empirical fractions around the true law across batches.

recall.question: How do you sample R, G, B from p_hat with uniform noise?
recall.answer: Draw u uniform in [0,1]. Return R if u < 0.5, G if u < 0.833, else B.

recall.question: Seed 0 gave counts (7,3,2). Is the sampler broken?
recall.answer: No. The fractions (0.583, 0.250, 0.167) wobble around the law. That wobble is sample noise, not a bug.

keyTerms.definition: L(theta) = p(data | theta): scores one parameter setting against fixed data.
The log of the likelihood; turns the product over IID draws into a sum.
Picking the parameters that make the observed data least surprising.

recall.question: Which law do the twelve draws prefer, and by how much?
recall.answer: p_hat over uniform q. Log-likelihoods -12.137 vs -13.183 nats: a 1.047 nat gap.

recall.question: In likelihood, what is fixed and what moves?
recall.answer: Data are fixed; parameters move. Maximum likelihood picks parameters that make the data least surprising.

keyTerms.definition: p_emp: mass 1/n on each observed sample; perfect memory, terrible model.
Empirical averages converge to expectations as n grows.

recall.question: Why does pure MLE memorize?
recall.answer: Maximum likelihood on a flexible model recovers the empirical distribution exactly.

recall.question: How fast did the Bernoulli(0.3) error shrink from n=12 to n=1200?
recall.answer: From 0.033 to 0.009, roughly like 1/sqrt(n).

keyTerms.definition: A function of the data that picks parameters.
Systematic error of an estimator.
Wobble of an estimate across datasets.
The property that estimation error vanishes as n grows.
Maximum likelihood estimation: picks parameters maximizing p(data | theta).

recall.question: What is the categorical MLE for the toy, and what goes wrong at n=1?
recall.answer: theta_hat = counts/n = (0.5, 0.333, 0.167). At n=1 with one red draw, the MLE says P(R) = 1: reckless at small n.

recall.question: How does the MLE standard deviation scale with n?
recall.answer: Like 1/sqrt(n): 0.143 at n=12, 0.014 at n=1200 in the simulation.

keyTerms.definition: H(p) = -E_p[log p(x)]: expected surprise; measures spread.
The unit of entropy with natural log; divide by ln 2 for bits.
H(p,q) = -sum p log q: the cost of coding p under model q.

recall.question: What is the toy's entropy, and the fair 3-sided law's?
recall.answer: Toy: 1.011 nats. Fair 3-sided: ln 3 = 1.099 nats. Uniform maximizes entropy.

recall.question: What is the 0.088 nat gap between cross-entropy and entropy?
recall.answer: The KL divergence, computed next.

keyTerms.definition: D_KL(p||q) = E_p[log p - log q]: the gap between cross-entropy and entropy.
D_KL(p||q): punishes q for missing data modes.
D_KL(q||p): punishes q for covering empty space.

recall.question: Is KL symmetric? Give the toy numbers.
recall.answer: No. KL(p_hat||uniform) = 0.087 nats; reversed = 0.096 nats.

recall.question: Why does minimizing cross-entropy equal minimizing forward KL?
recall.answer: KL = H(p,q) - H(p), and H(p) is constant in q. That identity is the whole of likelihood training.

keyTerms.definition: Distinct parameters give distinct observable laws.
Different parameters produce the same observable law.
A parameter transformation the data cannot see, e.g. label swaps.

recall.question: Give the label-swap example of non-identifiability.
recall.answer: A mixture of two identical Gaussians with weights (0.5,0.5). Swapping labels gives the same density, so likelihood cannot tell them apart.

recall.question: If parameters are non-identifiable, can prediction still work?
recall.answer: Yes. The parameter estimate wobbles between equivalent settings while predictions stay fixed.

B5 asks for its definition and the log-likelihood of twelve draws under the uniform law.
B3 asks for Z on scores (6,4,2) and the normalized law.

recall.question: Which ladder tests entropy and coding, and what does it cover?
recall.answer: L1. Define entropy, compute H for (0.5,0.25,0.25), explain why uniform maximizes it, relate cross-entropy to KL, and design a code.

recall.question: What does B3 ask?
recall.answer: Write the partition function Z for scores (6,4,2) and the normalized law.
